Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette: Arthur Vance was forty-five when the long winter of captivity ended, but the memory of it still dictated his days. For seventeen days, he had been held in a windowless concrete cellar, his wrists bound so tightly that a persistent ache settled deep in his neck. His captor moved through the darkness with heavy boots, frequently gripping Arthur’s shoulders and neck to check the ropes, and carried a bottle of cheap whiskey that left a thick, chemical tang in the damp air. The sudden slam of the steel door or the clatter of keys always preceded a shout or a blow. When police finally broke the lock, the release was not clean. His neck throbbed with the old tightness, his skin flinched at the weight of an officer’s hand on his arm, and the smell of spilled liquor on the man’s jacket sent him reeling. In the months that followed, Arthur found himself living in a state of perpetual readiness. His ears never rested. He was on high alert when hearing unexpected or loud sounds, dropping his notebook when a car backfired on the way to the newsroom and pressing himself against the curb until his heart slowed. He reacted as if danger were always circling, even when the city streets were quiet and the sun was high. His body remained superalert, watching for threats that never materialized. What frightened him most was how quickly his mind betrayed him. The memories of the cellar forced their way into his thoughts when he did not want them there. He would be reviewing copy for an investigative piece, and the footage of the concrete walls, the heavy footsteps, the clinking bottle, would play over and over behind his eyes. Remembering the event brought back the same terror he had felt in the dark, thick and suffocating, until he had to push his chair back and pace the room to steady his breathing. Over the following weeks and months, his daily routines shifted. Arthur stopped attending press mixers. The first time he walked into a crowded gallery opening, the smell of scotch and wine from passing trays hit him like a physical blow. He stepped outside, his neck muscles locking, convinced the air itself had shifted. He began declining assignments that required networking, choosing instead to file reports from his home office. He stopped shaking hands with sources, flinching at the brush of fingers, and retreated from his wife, Elena, when she reached for him on the couch. Their conversations grew stilted. He missed the regional journalism awards because he could not bear the thought of being in a room full of people he could not predict. The work he used to love became a source of dread, and the distance between him and Elena widened into a quiet, unspoken rift. It was the silence in their bedroom that finally pushed Arthur to seek help. He no longer recognized the man staring back at him in the mirror—jittery, exhausted, always scanning the corners of the room. He had come to the clinic after another panic attack at a deadline, his neck so tight it felt like it would snap, his thoughts trapped in the cellar’s repeating sequence. He did not know how to break the cycle or restore the life he had lost. What he hoped for was simply to sleep through the night without bracing for a door to open, and to sit across from his wife again without waiting for the other shoe to drop. He wanted to know if the past could ever stop dictating his present.
